vignette: Elias sits on the edge of his recliner, hands resting on his knees, eyes fixed on the window. Outside, a delivery truck backfires. His shoulders snap up, breath catches, and for three seconds he is twenty-eight again, standing on the slick deck of the USCGC Meridian, coughing through a thick, sweet-smelling cloud that rolled off a ruptured industrial tanker. The foremen had called it a routine coolant flush. The supplied masks had torn at the seams. Elias remembers the chemical burn in his throat, the way his lungs refused to empty, the medevac chopper’s rotors drowning out the captain’s orders. He doesn’t remember signing the paperwork afterward, only the long drive to the clinic and the white coat that said observation before everything else was filed away. Decades pass. Elias marries Miriam in ’84. They buy a house near the coast, not out of nostalgia, but because the salt air makes breathing easier, he tells himself. The Coast Guard retires him at fifty-two with a pension and a disability rating that feels like a quiet apology. He learns to live with the cough that never fully leaves him, the sleep that fractures into short, gasping pieces. At night, he wakes to the phantom smell of industrial solvent and checks the door locks three times. In the morning, he pours black coffee, watches the street, and wonders if the mail carrier is really a threat or just a man with a canvas bag. Miriam stops asking why he jumps at the microwave’s beep. She learns to walk softly, to keep the windows shut when the wind shifts west. Their son visits less often, unable to bear the careful, airless routine of their kitchen. Now, at seventy-two, Elias’s hands tremble when he signs his grocery receipts. His life was built on four decades of Coast Guard duty, yet the ocean view from his porch now triggers a tightness behind his ribs that feels like drowning. He is an African American man who spent his working life protecting maritime waters, but the checklist his new doctor handed him leaves him sitting in the quiet after the pen is capped. Seventy-six points. The number sits in his gut like a stone. He does not need a score to know he is fractured. He knows it in the way he flinches when a neighbor’s leaf blower kicks on, in the way he maps exit routes at the pharmacy, in the sudden cold sweat that breaks out when the radio plays a song from the ship’s mess hall. He tells Miriam he is fine over dinner, but his fork stays still. His thoughts loop on the same three days in October, replaying the rupture, the rush, the way his partner’s face turned gray under the mask. He stops going to the community center after the boiler room alarm tests. He buys industrial air purifiers, stacks them like talismans in the living room. At night, he lies awake counting the seconds between heartbeats, waiting for the next shift in the air, his body still braced for a sea that will not come.
